questions.q: What is the programme mainly about?
options: How to take good photos of wild animals in Africa
Why chimpanzees are in danger in Tanzania today
Jane Goodall's discoveries about how chimps are like us
The long history of National Geographic magazine
questions.why: They hear Jane Goodall reflect on the deep connections science has found between humans and great apes.

questions.q: What made Jane Goodall famous in 1965?
options: Appearing on the cover of National Geographic
Writing a best-selling book about her life
Winning an important international science prize
Appearing on a popular BBC radio programme
questions.why: Sam says she shot to fame in 1965 when she appeared on the cover of National Geographic.

questions.q: What did most scientists believe when Jane first went to Tanzania?
options: Chimps had no emotions at all
Chimps lived alone, not in families
Chimps could understand human language
Only humans could make and use tools
questions.why: Rob says most scientists believed the only animals capable of making and using tools were humans.

questions.q: What did Jane see the chimp Greybeard do?
options: Use a heavy stone to break open some nuts
Take the leaves off a twig to collect termites
Build a shelter from branches before it rained
Teach the young chimps how to climb tall trees
questions.why: She saw him strip the leaves from a twig and use grass stems to pull termites out of a mound.

questions.q: Why was Greybeard's behaviour so important?
options: It showed chimps prefer termites to fruit
It showed chimps copy humans
It proved wild animals could make their own tools
It showed chimps were becoming dangerous
questions.why: Rob says it was believed animals couldn't make tools, so this was proof of their intelligence.

questions.q: How did Jane feel about chimps having emotions like humans?
options: She wasn't surprised by it
She was shocked by it
She didn't believe it at first
She thought it was only true of young chimps
questions.why: She says, “I wasn't surprised that chimps had these emotions.”

questions.q: According to Jane, why do chimps seek physical contact?
options: To show who is the leader
To reduce nervousness or stress
To keep warm at night
To find food more easily
questions.why: She says they seek physical contact to alleviate nervousness or stress.

questions.q: What does Jane suggest about chimps' gestures like kissing and holding hands?
options: They are learned from people
They only happen in zoos
They are hard to understand without training
They are very similar to ours
questions.why: She says you can watch them without knowing anything about them, and 'it's so like us.'
